name: Sofpironium
lead: Sofpironium bromide is a topical anticholinergic gel developed by Bodor Laboratories and licensed to Brickell Biotech for primary axillary hyperhidrosis (excessive underarm sweating). It is designed to reduce sweating by blocking M3 muscarinic receptors in eccrine glands at the application site.[4] It received its first approval in Japan in September 2020 under the brand name Ecclock.[4]

In the United States the product is sold as Sofdra, and its label lists the indication as primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and pediatric patients aged 9 years and older.[6] Its relevance to appearance is indirect: underarm sweat is a grooming and clothing concern, and the gel is a prescription medicine for a recognised medical condition rather than a cosmetic product.
Randomized trials have compared the gel with vehicle (an inactive gel).[1][2] Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention are listed on the US label.[6]
infobox: Bodor Laboratories; licensed to Brickell Biotech[4]

paras: The US label indicates sofpironium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and children aged 9 and over.[6] A registered phase 2 trial has also examined the gel in palmar (hand) hyperhidrosis.[7]
Sofpironium is a competitive inhibitor of acetylcholine receptors on peripheral tissues, including sweat glands, and so indirectly lowers the rate of sweating.[6]

The label lists the most common adverse reactions (incidence of 2% or more) as dry mouth, blurred vision, application site pain, application site redness, dilated pupils, application site dermatitis, itching, urinary retention and application site irritation.[6] Warnings include urinary retention, the possibility of a generalized lack of sweating in hot environments, and effects on activities such as operating machinery.[6] No human pregnancy data are available; animal reproduction studies at the doses tested showed no significant adverse effects.[6]

A Japanese phase 3, vehicle-controlled trial of 5% sofpironium gel over 6 weeks used a combined primary endpoint of a Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Score of 1 or 2 plus at least a 50% reduction in gravimetric sweat weight.[1] A 52-week open-label extension in Japanese patients assessed longer-term safety and efficacy.[3] A US phase 2 randomized, double-blind trial tested three dosages against vehicle over 42 days.[2] Further phase 3 trials in the US are registered.[8] A 2025 systematic review has summarized efficacy and safety in primary hyperhidrosis.[5]

timeline.event: First approval of sofpironium bromide gel 5% in Japan for primary axillary hyperhidrosis.[4]

card.summary: Prescription topical anticholinergic gel for underarm sweating; trial-backed for hyperhidrosis, not a cosmetic.
card.note: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention) are listed on the label.

quick.overview:
Sofpironium is a prescription gel applied to the underarms to reduce excessive sweating (primary axillary hyperhidrosis). It was first approved in Japan in 2020 and is sold in the US as Sofdra.

It relates to appearance only indirectly, as a grooming-adjacent medical treatment; no looksmaxxing community discussion is documented.
quick.mechanism: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on sweat glands where it is applied, reducing the signal that triggers sweating.[4][6]
quick.risks: Label-listed adverse reactions include dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils, skin irritation and urinary retention; the label also warns about lack of sweating in hot conditions.[6]
